h1
Zeus had a headache. Then someone took an axe to it.
h2
His head split open, and out jumped a goddess in full armor, already shouting.
h3
That goddess is Athena. Every source we'll look at today agrees she came out of her father's head.
h4
What they can't agree on is who swung the axe. Or what happened to her mother, who in one version never left.
h5
So today we line up the suspects. Using the oldest poems we have, a jar from Athens, and the most famous temple in Greece.
a1
Quick reminder. Last time, Zeus swallowed his first wife, Metis, when she was about to give birth to Athena.
a2
Which leaves a puzzle. If the mother is inside Zeus, how does the baby get out?
a3
Hesiod's answer takes one line. Zeus himself gave birth to her, from his own head.
a4
That's it. He doesn't say how. He doesn't say it hurt.
a5
And then he moves straight on to Hera, who is very angry, and quarrelling with her husband.
a6
Hera has a child of her own, without Zeus. That child is Hephaestus, the best craftsman among the gods.
a7
Keep him in mind. He's going to matter.
b1
Now, some old copies of the poem carry a longer version of this passage. Scholars aren't sure Hesiod wrote it. But it's old, and it tells a very different story about Metis.
b2
In this version, Metis gets pregnant after Zeus swallows her. Inside him.
b3
Zeus gives birth by way of his head, on the banks of a river called Trito.
b4
And Metis never comes out. She stays hidden in his insides, wiser than gods and men.
b5
In there, the poem says, Athena gets the thing that will make her stronger than any other god. Zeus brings her out already dressed for war.
b6
So the wisest being alive is sitting inside the king of the gods.
b7
And honestly, the main version hints at the same idea. Hesiod says Zeus put Metis in his belly so that she could advise him, on good and on evil.
c1
So where does the axe come from? Not from Hesiod.
c2
More than two hundred years later, a poet called Pindar wrote a victory song for a boxer from the island of Rhodes.
c3
Why would a boxing song bring up Athena's birth? Because Rhodes had its own story about that day.
c4
By the craft of Hephaestus, with a bronze axe, Athena leapt from the crown of her father's head and cried aloud. And heaven trembled at her coming, and Mother Earth.
c4b
At that moment, the sun god told his sons on Rhodes to build Athena an altar, and be the first to honor her.
c4c
They hurried up the hill. And they forgot to bring fire. So they made their offerings without a flame.
c4d
Zeus rained gold on them anyway, and Athena made them the best craftsmen on earth. A flattering story to sing to a crowd from Rhodes.
c5
But look at the name in that song. Hephaestus, the smith. Our first suspect.
c6
But go back to Hesiod for a second. If you read his poem in order, Athena is born first. Hephaestus comes after, out of Hera's anger.
c7
Read that way, the smith couldn't have held the axe. He wasn't born yet.
c8
Pindar didn't seem to care. And he wasn't the last to name somebody else.
c9
Centuries later, a handbook of Greek myths called the Library gives the job to Prometheus. Or, it adds, as others say, Hephaestus.
Two suspects, and the handbook won't pick one. It does name the place, though. The river Triton.
d1
What did the birth actually look like? For that we have a short hymn to Athena, one of the Homeric Hymns, old poems written in the style of Homer.
d2
Athena springs from the immortal head and stands before Zeus, shaking a sharp spear.
d3
Awe takes hold of every god watching.
d4
Great Olympus reels at her strength. The earth around cries out, and the sea is tossed with dark waves.
d5
Even the sun stops. The sun god holds his horses still for a long while, until Athena takes the armor off her shoulders.
d6
And Zeus, the hymn says, is glad.
d7
This version has no axe in it at all, and nobody seems to be in pain. Zeus is simply proud.
e1
That's the poetry. Now the evidence you can actually go and see.
e2
This jar was painted in Athens, somewhere between five hundred and fifty and five hundred and twenty-five B.C. Today it's in the Louvre, in Paris.
e3
Look at the top of Zeus's head. That small figure in a helmet, already armed, is Athena.
e4
The woman on the right is a mystery. Some descriptions call her the goddess of childbirth. Others call her Aphrodite.
e5
About a century later, Athens put the same moment somewhere much bigger.
e6
The Parthenon, the great temple of Athena on the Acropolis. When the traveller Pausanias visited, he wrote that the sculptures over the entrance all showed the birth of Athena.
e7
Her birth, carved over the front door of her own city's greatest temple.
f1
So, who split Zeus's head open?
f2
Hesiod doesn't need anyone. Pindar says Hephaestus. The handbook says Prometheus, or maybe Hephaestus. And the hymn never mentions an axe.
f3
If you ask me, the axe was never the point.
f4
Look at what the oldest version keeps. Zeus swallows the wisest being alive. She stays inside him, giving advice. And his daughter, as strong as he is and just as wise, comes out of his head.
f5
That's my reading, not Hesiod's words. But it's hard to miss what the story is doing. It shows where the king of the gods keeps his best ideas.
f6
Next time: our other suspect. Prometheus, the Titan who tricked Zeus, and the woman the gods made because of it.
